meta_title: NCERT Exemplar Class 12 Integration Q44 Solved + Quiz
meta_desc: Solve NCERT Exemplar Class 12 integration Q44 by dividing by cos-squared and substituting t = tan x, then test the method with a free 8-question quiz.

quiz.title: Integrating a²cos²x + b²sin²x Denominators Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions on the divide-by-cos²x and t = tan x method used to crack integrals of the form ∫ dx / (a²cos²x + b²sin²x). Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Definite integration of a²cos²x + b²sin²x type denominators

questions.q: Dividing the numerator and denominator of ∫ dx / (a²cos²x + b²sin²x) by cos²x gives which integral?
questions.explanation: Dividing top and bottom by cos²x turns 1 in the numerator into sec²x, a²cos²x into a², and b²sin²x into b²tan²x. That is exactly the shape the t = tan x substitution needs.

questions.q: With the substitution t = tan x, what is dt?
questions.explanation: The derivative of tan x is sec²x, so dt = sec²x dx. This is why the sec²x created in the numerator is so convenient — it becomes dt outright.

questions.q: After substituting, the integral becomes ∫ dt / (a² + b²t²). What is its antiderivative?
questions.explanation: Write a² + b²t² = b²((a/b)² + t²). Using ∫ dt/(k² + t²) = (1/k) tan⁻¹(t/k) with k = a/b gives (1/ab) tan⁻¹(bt/a) + C.

questions.q: What is the value of ∫₀^(π/2) dx / (a²cos²x + b²sin²x)?
questions.explanation: As x runs from 0 to π/2, t = tan x runs from 0 to ∞. So (1/ab) tan⁻¹(bt/a) is evaluated from 0 to ∞, giving (1/ab)(π/2) = π/(2ab).

questions.q: Why is dividing through by cos²x the key first step for these integrals?
options: It manufactures a sec²x numerator so that t = tan x turns the whole thing into a standard 1/(a² + b²t²) form
It removes the constants a and b from the problem
It converts the definite limits into 0 and 1
It changes the integrand into a perfect square
questions.explanation: The single trick that unlocks the problem is producing sec²x on top. Once dt = sec²x dx is available, t = tan x collapses the trigonometric integral into a rational one you already know how to integrate.
Here a² = 1 and b² = 4, so a = 1 and b = 2. Using π/(2ab) gives π/(2 · 1 · 2) = π/4.

questions.q: Q44 asks for the squared denominator ∫₀^(π/2) dx / (a²cos²x + b²sin²x)². What is its value?
questions.explanation: Differentiating I = π/(2ab) with respect to a² gives ∫ cos²x dx/(…)² = π/(4a³b); with respect to b² gives ∫ sin²x dx/(…)² = π/(4ab³). Adding them (since cos²x + sin²x = 1) gives π(a² + b²)/(4a³b³).

questions.q: How is the squared-denominator result of Q44 obtained from the simpler integral I = π/(2ab)?
options: By integrating I once more from 0 to π/2
By multiplying I by a² + b²
By differentiating I with respect to the parameters a² and b² and adding the two results
questions.explanation: Treating a² and b² as parameters, ∂/∂(a²) and ∂/∂(b²) each pull down a factor and raise the denominator power to 2. Summing the two partial derivatives reconstructs cos²x + sin²x = 1 in the numerator, giving the squared integral directly.

faq.q: Which technique solves integrals like ∫ dx / (a²cos²x + b²sin²x)?
faq.a: Divide the numerator and denominator by cos²x to get a sec²x on top, then substitute t = tan x. The integral becomes ∫ dt/(a² + b²t²), a standard arctangent form.

faq.q: What is the value of ∫₀^(π/2) dx / (a²cos²x + b²sin²x)?
faq.a: It equals π/(2ab). As x goes from 0 to π/2, t = tan x goes from 0 to infinity, so the arctangent term evaluates to π/2 and the constant 1/(ab) sits outside.

faq.q: How do you handle the squared denominator in Q44?
faq.a: Start from the known result I = π/(2ab), treat a² and b² as parameters, and differentiate I with respect to each. Adding the two partial derivatives rebuilds cos²x + sin²x = 1 in the numerator and gives π(a² + b²)/(4a³b³).

faq.q: Why divide by cos²x rather than sin²x?
faq.a: Either works, but dividing by cos²x creates sec²x, whose integral pairs with t = tan x. Dividing by sin²x would create cosec²x and push you toward t = cot x with a sign to track, so cos²x is the tidier default.
